title: The Righteous Will Live by Faith
summary: Habakkuk takes his stand on the watchtower, and God answers: write the vision plainly, for it awaits its appointed time and will surely come. The proud one is not upright, but the righteous will live by faith. Five woes follow against the greedy conqueror, who plunders nations, builds by unjust gain and bloodshed, shames his neighbors, and trusts lifeless idols, and the chapter ends with the LORD in his holy temple and all the earth called to silence.
story: In chapter 1, Habakkuk asked why God tolerated injustice in Judah and was told that Babylon was coming; then he asked how a holy God could use Babylon. This chapter is God's answer to that second question. It does not explain everything. It gives a promise, that God's plan has a time and will not fail; a contrast, between the swollen pride of the conqueror and the faithful endurance of the righteous; and a verdict, that Babylon's own crimes will bring it down. The chapter's final verse, calling the whole earth to silence before God in his temple, prepares for chapter 3, where Habakkuk moves from argument to prayer.
historical:
Habakkuk wrote as Babylon rose to dominate the Near East in the late seventh century BC. After destroying Nineveh in 612 BC and defeating Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC, the Babylonian empire under Nebuchadnezzar extended its control over Syria, Phoenicia, and Judah, deporting populations and collecting tribute. Babylon's building projects were famous: Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt the city on a grand scale, with massive walls, palaces, and temples, largely financed by the wealth of conquered peoples. The woes of this chapter, against one who amasses what is not his, builds by unjust gain, and establishes a town by iniquity, fit that empire closely. The references to violence against Lebanon in verse 17 recall the cutting of Lebanon's cedars for imperial building, something Mesopotamian kings boasted of in their inscriptions.

The promised end came in 539 BC, when Cyrus of Persia took Babylon. Habakkuk did not live to see it, and the chapter's insistence that the vision awaits an appointed time reflects the long wait of those who trusted it.
cultural:
Verses 1 and 2 draw on two familiar practices. City walls had watchtowers where sentries looked for approaching messengers or armies, and Habakkuk pictures himself as such a watchman, waiting for God's word. Public announcements were inscribed on tablets of clay, stone, or wood so that they could be read and carried. The phrase so that a herald may run with it probably means that the message should be plain enough for a messenger to read and deliver, or for anyone to read at a glance as they pass by.

The woes use the form of a taunt song, a proverb or mocking saying (mashal) that the nations take up against their oppressor. Several images belong to ancient economic life. Many loans and creditors who suddenly arise (verses 6 and 7) evoke the practice of debt and pledge, turned here against the conqueror, whose victims become his creditors. Giving a neighbor drink to gaze on his nakedness (verse 15) pictures deliberate humiliation, and the cup in the LORD's right hand draws on the prophetic image of the cup of God's wrath (Jeremiah 25:15). Idols were carved of wood or cast in metal and overlaid with gold and silver, and the scorn of verses 18 and 19 for an image that cannot speak or breathe echoes Isaiah 44 and Psalm 115.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 5 contain the prophet's watch and God's answer, centered on verse 4, where the proud one and the righteous one are set side by side in two short, dense lines. Verses 6 to 20 contain five woe oracles (verses 6, 9, 12, 15, and 19), each opening with the cry woe to him who, naming a crime, and announcing a fitting consequence. The punishments mirror the crimes: the plunderer is plundered, the house built by unjust gain is shamed, the drunkard-maker must drink. Two verses stand outside the woe pattern and interpret it: verse 14, promising that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, and verse 20, the LORD in his holy temple. These stand in contrast to the self-made glory of the conqueror and the dumb idols of the final woe.

outline.t: Write the vision: it will surely come
Second woe: the house built by unjust gain
Third woe: the city built with bloodshed
Fourth woe: the one who shames his neighbors
Fifth woe: lifeless idols and the LORD in his temple

doctrines.note: Verse 4 sets the righteous person, who lives by faith or faithfulness, against the proud one whose soul is not upright. Faith here is steady trust in God's word that shows itself in a faithful life while waiting for God to act.

The five woes show God's judgment often working through the consequences of sin itself: the plunderer's victims rise against him, the violent house cries out, the idol fails its maker. God's justice is built into the moral order of his world.

The vision awaits an appointed time, and the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD. Hope in this chapter is patient confidence in a future God has promised, even when it lingers.
The final woe mocks the idol as a teacher of lies, overlaid with gold but without breath. In contrast, the living God is in his holy temple, and before him all the earth is silent.

words.note: Emunah, faithfulness, steadiness, trustworthiness. The word comes from the root that gives us amen, and it describes firmness, reliability, and loyal trust. In verse 4 the righteous live by their emunah, their faithful trust in God that holds steady through the coming disaster. The Greek translation used in the early church read by my faith or faithfulness, meaning God's; the New Testament quotations use pistis, which can mean both faith and faithfulness.

Tsaddiq, righteous, the person in right relationship with God and living by his standards. In Habakkuk 1 the righteous are hemmed in and swallowed by the wicked. In 2:4 they are promised life. Paul will use this verse to ask how anyone comes to be counted righteous before God.

Chayah, to live. In verse 4 it means more than survival: to endure, to have life under God's favor through the coming judgment. The contrast is with the proud conqueror whose appetite is like Sheol and Death, never satisfied.

Kavod, glory, from a root meaning heavy or weighty. It is used three times in the chapter. The conqueror seeks glory by violence but will be filled with shame instead of glory (verse 16), while the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD (verse 14). The chapter sets two kinds of glory against each other.

christ: Habakkuk 2:4 is one of the Old Testament verses most important to the New. Paul quotes it in Romans 1:17, where the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith, as it is written, “The righteous will live by faith.” He quotes it again in Galatians 3:11 to argue that “no one is justified before God by the law”. In both places he reads the verse as teaching that the righteous person is the one who lives by faith in God's promise, now fulfilled in Christ, rather than by performing the law. Hebrews 10:37-38 quotes the verse in a form close to the Greek translation, “But My righteous one will live by faith”, and joins it to verse 3, applying the promise that the vision will surely come and not delay to “He who is coming”, Christ at his return. Interpreters debate how directly these uses reflect the prophet's meaning. In Habakkuk the emphasis falls on faithful endurance; Paul stresses trust as the way into right standing with God; Hebrews stresses perseverance. Many see these as complementary: faithfulness is trust that persists. Among ancient Jewish readers, the Qumran community's commentary on Habakkuk applied the verse to those who kept the law and remained loyal to their Teacher of Righteousness. In the early sixteenth century, Martin Luther's rereading of Romans 1:17 put this verse at the heart of the Reformation. Verse 14's promise that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD also reaches its New Testament fulfillment in the spread of the gospel and the hope of the new creation.

hard.q: Did Paul use Habakkuk 2:4 fairly, when the prophet seems to be talking about faithfulness rather than faith in Christ?
hard.a: This is a real question in scholarship. The Hebrew word emunah usually means faithfulness, and in context Habakkuk contrasts the proud conqueror with the loyal Judean who trusts God through judgment. Some scholars argue that Paul shifted the meaning toward belief in the gospel. Others respond that in Hebrew thought trust and faithfulness are not separable: the faithful person is the one who trusts God's promise and so remains loyal. On this view Paul draws out what was already there, since Habakkuk's righteous one lives not by his own strength (like the proud Babylonian) but by reliance on God's word. A further debate concerns whose faithfulness is meant: the Hebrew says his, the Greek translation says my (God's), and some scholars read Paul's phrase from faith to faith as including God's or Christ's faithfulness as well as human trust. Christians agree that the verse speaks of a life resting on God rather than on self; they differ on how to weigh these emphases.

questions: God told Habakkuk that the vision would come at its appointed time, though it might linger. What are you waiting for God to do, and what helps you keep trusting while you wait?
Verse 4 contrasts the proud person with the one who lives by faith. What does it look like in ordinary life to live by trust in God rather than by self-reliance?
The woes show evil bringing its own consequences. Have you seen greed or violence undo itself? What does that suggest about the way God has made the world?
